\section{Results}

\subsection{Experimental setup}

All measurements were taken on an Intel Core i9-7900X (Skylake-X, AVX-512), its ten cores at a fixed 3.3~GHz with turbo boost and hyper-threading disabled, with dinara-align compiled by Mojo 1.1.0 \citep{Modular2025mojo} at commit \texttt{87d365f} and every tool compiled for the native instruction set except BSAlign's gap-affine kernel, which its own build keeps to SSE4.2. We combined the protocols of A*PA2 \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2} and QuickEd \citep{Doblas2025quicked}.

The real datasets come from both. From A*PA2's release \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024pabench} we use the nanopore sets ont-1k, ont-10k, ont-50k and ont-500k, named by length class (mean 0.83, 3.6, 9.6 and 642~kbp), CHM13 reads paired with the CHM13 reference; ont-500k-genvar, ultra-long reads of another individual against the same reference, which adds genetic variation and gaps of up to 42~kbp; and 30~kbp SARS-CoV-2 genomes. We call the two 500k sets ultra-long. For QuickEd's Illumina 2$\times$250~bp, PacBio HiFi and nanopore PromethION technologies we use HG002 reads from Genome in a Bottle \citep{Zook2016giab}: Illumina and HiFi reads of one region of chromosome 20, and UCSC's ultra-long PromethION reads \citep{Shafin2020shasta} of one region of chromosome 12, of 10~kbp or more as in QuickEd's set (ont-promethion; 45~kbp on average in the sample, up to 156~kbp). Each read was picked with mapping quality at least 20 on GRCh38, mapped by minimap2 \citep{Li2018minimap2} to both haplotypes of HG002's own assembly \citep{Hansen2025hg002} and paired with the stretch it covers, its soft-clipped ends trimmed, so that pairs differ mainly by sequencing errors. The simulated datasets are QuickEd's random sequences \citep{Doblas2024datasets} of 10~kbp to 1~Mbp whose pairs differ by single-base substitutions, insertions and deletions spread uniformly at nominal error rates of 1, 5, 10 and 20\%, modelling no sequencing technology; the 20\% sets measure 17\% divergence (Supplementary Table S6).

Each dataset was sampled to about 2~Mbp of sequence, both sides counted, and at least four pairs. Every tool aligned each pair with traceback, on one pinned core, through one aligner object per sample as its own benchmark runner does, with a 30~s budget per sample, in three rounds that alternated between the tools; a pair's time is its median over the rounds, and a tool is credited only with the pairs it completed in every round. The rounds agreed closely: the median spread between a tool's fastest and slowest round was 0.5\% at unit and 0.7\% at gap-affine costs, at most 18\%, on dinara-align's 0.6~\textmu s Illumina alignments. Timings quoted in Section 3 were recorded when each change was made, against the version before it (Supplementary Table S1). The exact aligners compared are A*PA2-full (with the seed heuristic and pruning) and A*PA2-simple (band doubling alone), A*PA \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}, Edlib \citep{Sosic2017edlib}, WFA and BiWFA, which denote WFA2-lib in its high-memory and bidirectional modes \citep{MarcoSola2021wfa,MarcoSola2023biwfa}, QuickEd, BSAlign \citep{Shao2024bsalign}, KSW2 \citep{Li2018minimap2}, parasail \citep{Daily2016parasail} and SSW \citep{Zhao2013ssw}, each on the workloads it supports. On the pairs any two tools completed, their costs agreed, and at unit costs they agreed with the published A*PA2 results on its datasets. The other alignment modes were timed in-process on simulated workloads, and the batches on 500{,}000 simulated pairs of 148~bp at 1\% error, each the median of three runs (Supplementary Tables S3 and S8).

\subsection{Speed and memory}

At unit costs dinara-align had the lowest mean time per alignment of the exact aligners on all 25 datasets. On the real data (Table~\ref{tab:unit}) it was 1.4 to 2.4 times faster than the fastest alternative on the nanopore reads (1.7 times on PromethION) and 2.6 times on the SARS-CoV-2 genomes, and 1.9 and 5.1 times faster than WFA, the fastest of the others there, on the Illumina and HiFi reads. On the simulated data (Fig.~\ref{fig:sweeps}; Supplementary Table S5) it was 1.1 to 2.4 times faster than the fastest alternative: 100~kbp pairs at 1, 5, 10 and 20\% errors took 1.5, 5.1, 7.2 and 15.8~ms, against 7.5, 8.4, 13.9 and 36.8~ms for A*PA2-full and 12.5, 23.9, 39.0 and 62.6~ms for QuickEd. Its narrowest margin was on 10~kbp pairs at 5\%, 0.268 against 0.288~ms for A*PA2-simple. Over all 25 datasets QuickEd took 3.0 to 74 times as long, 7.8 times in the geometric mean.

At gap-affine costs dinara-align was 1.02 to 3.3 times faster than the faster of WFA and BiWFA on the 16 datasets all three completed (Table~\ref{tab:affine}; Supplementary Table S4), the lowest on the Illumina reads, 1.51 against 1.54~\textmu s for WFA, a tie within the spread of its rounds. It aligned every PromethION pair, in 286~ms against 576~ms for BiWFA, where WFA ran out of memory after 7 of 22, and completed more of the simulated pairs of 100~kbp or more than any other tool, 45 against 41 for BiWFA; but it completed no ont-500k read and one of the four ont-500k-genvar reads. In the other modes it was as fast as, or up to 22 times faster than, the fastest tool offering the same mode, infix alignment at (4, 6, 2) being a tie (Supplementary Table S3). Global scores of 500{,}000 short-read pairs took 231~ms on one core and 29~ms on ten at (1, 2, 1), 4.6 and 3.9 times faster than WFA2-lib (Supplementary Table S8).

An alignment of an ultra-long read increased peak memory by at most 48 MiB, against 81 MiB for A*PA2-full, and of a 1~Mbp pair at 20\% errors by at most 123 MiB, against 184 MiB (Supplementary Table S7). This growth includes the seed heuristic and the band; the stored tile boundaries stayed within the default limit of 80 MiB (Section 3.7). QuickEd stayed near 25 MiB. On short reads dinara-align's peak was higher than the others' (Table~\ref{tab:unit}): the Mojo runtime and the sample, read whole, take about 13 MiB.
